newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coup leader tells why he took power.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coup leader tells why he took power.

text.p: Sierra Leone coup leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah said on Friday that he seized power in order to end six years of civil war, and that he planned to form a broad-based government in which rebels played a full part.

Koromah told Reuters Television in his first formal interview with foreign press since the May 25 coup that the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) rebels and the army were tired of fighting and wanted peace.

He also accused ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, whose 1996 election ended four years of army rule, of undermining the honour and dignity of the armed forces by turning a militia of Kamajor traditional hunters against them.
"Our intention is to form a broad based government of national unity fully incorporating the RUF to restore everlasting peace and sanity throughout the country," he said.

"The deal we can do is for all the parties in Sierra Leone -- that is (for) the politicians, the servicemen and people to sit together and decide the type off Sierra Leone we want for the 21st century," he added.

"We are committed to the democratic process and we want elections but there are problems that we have to solve. We must make sure that these problems are ironed out before there will be an election," he said, adding that this would take at least 18 months.
The coup has been widely condemned. The Organisation of African Unity summit in Zimbabwe urged Kabbah's reinstatement.
Regional giant Nigeria, which had troops in Sierra Leone under defence pact, has sent in reinforcements as part of West African efforts to restore Kabbah to power.

Dissident army officers have said they will not accept Kabbah back. Koromah said he wondered what sort of man Kabbah was if he wanted to come back and "rule over corpses and a destroyed city" -- a hint that he could only be reinstated by force.
"We are against foreign intervention as this is a domestic matter," he added.

Koromah said the organisers of the coup were able to control the rebels, who took up arms in 1991 and who flooded into the city after the coup. Previously they had got no further than the approaches to the city before being driven back by troops trained and helped by South African mercenaries.
"They (the rebels) are tired of fighting. We too are tired of fighting. We need peace and we want it now and we are going to get peace," Koromah said.
"They are committed to peace in Sierra Leone and the RUF has assured the new military regime through the RUF leader Corporal Foday Sankoh that they are committed to peace," he added.
Sankoh, who signed a fragile peace deal with Kabbah in November, is under virtual house arrest in Nigeria.
Sierra Leone is one of the world's poorest countries despite mineral wealth such as diamonds.
Koromah, who seized power with a group of junior officers, said there were many reasons for staging the coup, the third in five years.
"First and foremost we want to put an end to the continued bloodbath that characterised our civil war for the past six years, by bringing the RUF into our fold," he said.

"The ousted government has lost all credibility of resuscitating the peace process by attempting to divide and dictate to the RUF leadership which consequently led to the deadlock in the peace process," he added. "This situation sparked a fierce resumption of hostilities."

He said the coup's organisers wanted to "prevent the country from descending into tribal and regional warfare." He said the formation of the civil defence forces on regional and tribal lines would "no doubt have created disaster for this nation".

He also said the coup's organisers wanted to "restore the honour and dignity of the military" and accused the Kabbah government of deliberately trying to "sabotage the legitimacy of the military" by "arming and poisoning the minds" of the Kamajors.
"This situation led to the persistent slaughter of soldiers nationwide," he said, adding: "In spite of repeated complaints, the past government refused to take necessary action."
